explanations.explanation: This neuron lights up on the “meat” of a sentence—the principal content words (especially verbs or operation‐nouns) that name the core action or topic (e.g. drill, read, power, debounce, nacho).

This neuron is not about meaning at all but about word‐shape: it spikes on short, two-syllable (or disyllabic) letter sequences where consonants and vowels alternate (a CVCV-style pattern), e.g. “GA-with,” “RA-ving,” “FI-gure,” “VA-tal,” “EASE,” “DO,” etc.
This feature fires on the “scheme‐separator” pattern in URIs (the “protocol://…” tokens such as http://, https://, jar://, php://, file://, etc.).
This neuron detects the period ('.') token when it serves as trailing punctuation—e.g. the final full-stop in titles, headings, sentences, or common abbreviations (Inc., Dr., Nov., St., etc.).

This feature picks out the little “flag” words in scientific writing that signal a study’s functions, relationships and causal or purposive moves—tokens like result, responsible, deal, limited, relationship, purpose, applications, play/played, sheds (light), determining, etc. In other words, it marks the discourse cues that frame goals, roles, outcomes and how concepts relate or lead to one another.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is simply a high‐frequency subword detector: it lights up on short, common tokens (especially function words like articles and pronouns – um, o, el, die, elle, here, its – but also very frequent content fragments like part, terms, area, ine) across many languages.

This neuron is a “section‐start” detector: it lights up on the first word or marker of a new headline/heading or content block (e.g. imperatives like “Stay …,” “Get …,” labels like “Video:,” or the opening token of a news snippet).

This neuron fires on the stem or first morpheme of compound technical and proper‐name expressions—e.g. “Visual-” (Visual Studio), “Real-” (real-time/estate), “Big-” (big data), “Elect-” (electrochemical), “Auto-” (Automatron), “Super-” (Supertech), “Inter-” (interhospital), etc.—marking the common root that kicks off multiword or branded terms.

This neuron is a detector for infrequent multi‐character subword fragments—those consonant-vowel-consonant (and longer) chunks like “perox,” “osp,” “pet,” “mit,” “io,” “iv,” etc.—that typically occur at morpheme boundaries in technical or scientific vocabulary.

explanations.explanation: This neuron is a “sentence‐ or segment‐start” detector: it spikes on the first contentful subword of a new sentence or heading (e.g. the “spir” of “Aspirants…,” the “not” in “If not…,” the “ways” of “Anyways…,” “Here,” “The goal,” “Regents,” “Services,” etc.). Essentially it flags the opening lexical item that follows a boundary (period, newline, heading marker).
